title: 《Digital Fairness Act》是一笔十年才到期的账单 | 观点
content:
The Digital Fairness Act is a decade-long bill coming due | Opinion | GamesIndustry.biz

When a draft of the European Commission's Digital Fairness Act leaked earlier this week, some industry reactions had a distinctly end-of-days flavour. The official responses now
winding their way out of trade bodies
after the official draft of the act was released are only ratcheting down the tone a little; less apocalyptic, but nonetheless grim warnings of a terrible fate for European games companies, muttering darkly about the stripping of supposed freedoms from players, parents, and everyone else within a very wide radius.
We've all known that the European Union has been gearing up to regulate in-game monetisation for around a decade at this point, so I don't know that "shock" is the right term for the reaction – but I do understand that there's a hare-and-tortoise element to national and supranational regulation that often catches high-tech industries, like gaming, off-guard.
While high-tech companies move fast and break things, they often lose sight of the regulators many, many steps behind, slowly and methodically totting up an account of all those broken things. Once regulations finally arrive, the business practices they limit seem baked-in and well-established to the fast-moving companies, who spit feathers at the notion that they can't do them anymore. Smartphones, app stores, and in-app purchases seem like old news to the games industry, making it easy to miss how very new and novel they are when viewed on a legislative and regulatory timescale.
The draft version of the EU's Digital Fairness Act was officially revealed on Wednesday  |
Image credit:
Marco on Unsplash
Dr Andreas Lober has
already done an excellent job on this site of walking through what the formal draft of the act actually contains, article by article
. I won't retread that ground. I will say that I understand – not sympathise with, perhaps, but certainly understand – why the wide-reaching restrictions in the proposed legislation feel like the sky is falling for a certain kind of games executive. If your earnings calls have been powered for years by mechanisms like loot boxes, virtual currencies, and engagement patterns designed to tickle people's FOMO instincts, this draft must read like a list of your business's load-bearing walls being marked for demolition.
What actually ends up being enacted after the draft legislation has been debated and amended remains to be seen, but as an opening salvo, this is an aggressive one – essentially a maximal set of regulatory demands. If nothing else, it implies a significant rift between the Commission and the industry it is regulating here – which raises two pertinent broader questions. How on earth did we end up here, with the industry so utterly at loggerheads with the world's most powerful regulatory body, and where does it all go next?
The first question, at least, has a fairly simple answer. This is a tragedy of the commons: one that's been playing out in slow motion for well over a decade.
It was inevitable that the issue would eventually be taken up at a European level
Regulators across Europe have been very vocally uncomfortable with the monetisation mechanisms creeping into games since at least the early 2010s – especially those aimed at, or simply accessible to, children. Once national legislators and regulators started picking off the most egregious practices piecemeal – Belgium's gaming commission
declaring paid loot boxes to be illegal gambling in 2018
being the most famous example, but far from the only one – it was inevitable that the issue would eventually be taken up at a European level. A patchwork of national rules across a single market is precisely the kind of problem the EU exists to solve, and by 2023 the European Parliament was calling for a harmonised approach to loot boxes.
As this process rolled slowly forwards, there were plenty of warnings about where this would lead – many of them from developers and publishers with skin in the game. The message was consistent: if this ends up being decided in Brussels, the rules that come down will be stricter than anyone in the industry wants. EU regulation is powerful, and from a consumer's perspective, it's frequently welcome (one sobering reality check for anyone hoping that this act will be watered down significantly is to look at comments about it from consumers online, and see where the balance of opinion among ordinary citizens lies). It's also, much of the time, a blunt instrument. A framework that has to function across 27 member states, and which in the case of the Digital Fairness Act also has to cover subscription traps, influencer marketing, customer service, and the interface design of practically every consumer-facing website and app, is going to sacrifice nuance in a lot of places along the way.
PEGI said it would begin rating games with loot boxes as 16+ earlier this year  |
Image credit:
PEGI
This is one of the major problems facing the lobbying efforts that will now attempt to dial down some of the strictest parts of the act: games are one stakeholder among many, and may not be one with a great deal of goodwill in the bank.
Why not? In part, because regulators tend to view the games business as being something of an offshoot of the tech business, and the EU has made clear how little time it has for tech giants and their machinations in recent years. It's also, however, undeniable that there was a time when a genuine effort at industry self-regulation might plausibly have headed off the sharper end of the EU's interest. What we got instead was
lip-service so transparent it was practically see-through
. Drop-rate disclosures arrived grudgingly, often tucked away where few players would ever see them (I especially like the games that show every other piece of information in the in-game UI, but cannot
